title: Recognising white muscle disease in lambs
subtitle: Understanding selenium and vitamin E deficiency as the cause of stiff, weak, or sudden-death lambs.
excerpt: White muscle disease is a degenerative muscle condition in newborn and young lambs caused by selenium or vitamin E deficiency, or both. It produces sudden death in the days around birth, or a characteristic stiff, arched-back, weak-legged gait in lambs that survive the neonatal period. It is entirely preventable and responds to treatment if caught early, but kills quickly once the heart muscle is affected.

glossaryTerms.definition: Nutritional muscular dystrophy in lambs caused by selenium or vitamin E deficiency. Affected muscle fibres die and are replaced by pale fibrous tissue — visible as white streaks when the carcass is examined. In cardiac muscle, it causes sudden death.

A shortage of the trace element selenium in the diet, most common on acidic, high-rainfall soils or on land with high sulphur inputs. Selenium is used in antioxidant enzyme systems and muscle function. Sheep are sensitive to both deficiency and toxicity.

content.text: in lambs has two forms. The cardiac form causes sudden death in the neonatal period. The subacute form shows up in the first six weeks as stiff, stilted movement and inability to suckle. Both result from muscle tissue damage caused by

Cardiac form: lambs born apparently normal but found dead within 48 hours. Several lambs from different ewes dying at the same time in the first days after birth, without obvious trauma or hypothermia, should raise suspicion.
Skeletal muscle form: lambs at one to six weeks that move with a stiff, paddling gait, arch the back, and have difficulty rising after lying down. Hindquarters are most obviously affected.
Affected lambs may be unable to suckle due to tongue and jaw muscle weakness.
In later stages the condition can look like joint ill, spinal abscess, or arthritis. Blood tests for selenium and creatine kinase, or muscle checks after death, confirm the diagnosis.

Selenium is poorly available on acidic, high-rainfall soils and on sandy or peaty soils. White muscle disease is most common in the uplands of Wales, Scotland, and the Pennines, and in some lowland areas with acid light soils. High sulphur from pollution or fertilisers can block selenium uptake even where soil levels look adequate.

Affected lambs receive a combined selenium and vitamin E injection, available as a licensed veterinary product. Dosage is by weight and is supplied under a vet prescription. Treatment in the skeletal muscle form, if caught before extensive muscle damage, produces recovery over several days. The cardiac form is not survivable once the heart is severely involved.
Prevention is the effective strategy: cure of the cardiac form is almost never possible, and skeletal muscle damage takes weeks to recover from even with treatment. Prevention routes:
A combined selenium and vitamin E injection given to ewes four to six weeks before lambing. Crosses the placenta and gives lambs a selenium reserve from birth.
A trace element bolus given to ewes at mating, which releases selenium over several months.
Mineralised compound feed with selenium, fed to ewes in the eight weeks before lambing.

Selenium toxicity is a serious risk: the margin between deficiency and toxicity is narrower in sheep than in any other UK farm animal. Do not supplement with selenium-containing products without confirming deficiency through blood testing. Do not combine selenium-containing boluses with selenium injections without vet guidance.

attrs.cue: Multiple lambs dead in the first 48 hours with no obvious cause
attrs.cause: Cardiac white muscle disease in multiple lambs from selenium-deficient ewes
attrs.fix: Send a casualty for post-mortem. The white streaks in heart and skeletal muscle tissue are diagnostic. If confirmed, discuss emergency ewe supplementation and lamb treatment with your vet for the rest of lambing.

attrs.cue: Lamb treated with selenium injection is still stiff after five days
attrs.cause: Significant skeletal muscle damage already present before treatment
attrs.fix: Continue supportive care: tube-feed if the lamb cannot suckle, keep warm and comfortable. Recovery from established skeletal muscle white muscle disease is slow. Re-evaluate with your vet at the one-week mark.
